rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samarrai distinguishes the causative verb’s verbal noun from the following noun of straying: Satan initiates misguidance, while people themselves complete and pursue it.
rows.anchor: لأن مصدر (أضلّ) : الإضلال أما الضلال فهو مصدر ضلّ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an shifts forms and levels of emphasis in superficially similar expressions according to the context and the degree of wonder.
rows.anchor: وقد يَستعملُ في كان ما صيغةً ثم يعدلُ في مكان آخر عن تلك الصيغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qaf, the plain description of the arrival of a messenger from among the people expresses the initial wonder without extra emphasis.
rows.anchor: فأنت ترى أنه قال في سورة ق: (هذا شيء عجيب)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sarah’s old age and barrenness, together with her elderly husband, make the conception more astonishing, so the verse emphasizes the wonder with inna and the lām.
rows.anchor: فإذا اجتمع إلى كل ذلك أن بلعها شيخ كان أبعدَ وأبعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entrenched polytheists find exclusive worship of one God especially astonishing; inna, the lām, and ʿujāb intensify the response, with fuʿāl stronger than faʿīl.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن (فُعَالاً) أبلغ من (فَعِيل) عند العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrahim says barīʾ while investigating celestial bodies in uncertainty (6:78), but barāʾ while publicly preaching against his people’s worship (43:26–27); the latter is stronger.
rows.anchor: أما في الآية الثانية فهو في مقام التبليغ فقد أصبح نبياً مرسلاً من ربه أعلن حربه على الشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barāʾ, a verbal noun, is more forceful than the adjective barīʾ; the author illustrates noun force with ʿadl and sūʾ, and reads Noah’s son as having become a nonrighteous act (11:46).
rows.anchor: أن (براء) أقوى من بريء فإنها براءة بصيغة المصدر الذي هو الحدث المجرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added nūn in innanī barāʾ, which the author calls nūn al-wiqāya, adds emphasis in the Zukhruf formulation compared with innī barīʾ in al-Anʿām.
rows.anchor: فقال: (إنني براء) ولم يأت بها في آية الأنعام بل قال: (إني بريء)

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi describes the Qur’an as a cohesive whole, like one sūra or even one verse.
rows.anchor: وصدق الإمام الرازي إذ قال: القرآن كالسورة الواحدة بل كالآية الواحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿlān conveys a renewed or changing quality, whereas faʿīl conveys a stable one; Rahmān and Rahīm together affirm that God’s mercy is both permanent and continually renewed.
rows.anchor: فإن صيغة (فعلان) تفيد الحدوث والتجدد، وصيغة (فعيل) تفيد الثبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Baqara uses the plural of abundance, sanābil, in a context of multiplying reward, while Joseph uses the plural of paucity, sunbulāt, for seven ears without a need to stress abundance.
rows.anchor: وسِرُّ ذلك أن سنابل جمع كثرة وسنبلات جمع قلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham gives thanks for some of God’s blessings, hence the paucity plural anʿum; Luqman uses abundant niʿam when enumerating gifts, since people cannot count all blessings (16:18).
rows.anchor: فجمع النعمة في آية النحل جمع قلة (أنعُم) وجمعها في لقمان جمع كثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saba uses lā to deny the future coming of the Hour, while Yunus uses mā for present affairs and knowledge; each negator suits its context.
rows.anchor: أما النفي بـ (لا) في سبأ فلأن الكلام على الساعة، والساعة استقبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saba uses the pronoun because God has just been named as Lord and Knower of the unseen; Yunus names “your Lord” explicitly because no such mention precedes it.
rows.anchor: فجاء بالضمير في سبأ لأنه تقدم ذكر الرب عالم الغيب فيها فأعاد الضمير عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yunus adds min as an emphatic exhaustive particle because the passage foregrounds God’s comprehensive knowledge; in Saba, knowledge of the unseen follows mention of the Hour.
rows.anchor: ناسب ذلك زيادة (من) الاستغراقية المؤكدة التي تستغرق كل مذكور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saba puts the heavens first because the Hour’s events begin in heaven and affect heaven’s inhabitants, as the trumpet passages illustrate.
rows.anchor: فلأن الكلام على الساعة وأمرها يأتي من السماء وهي تبدأ بأهل السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yunus puts earth first because the preceding context concerns people’s circumstances, recitation, and deeds on earth.
rows.anchor: فناسب ذلك تقديم الأرض في آية يونس

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf notes that, although heaven normally precedes earth, the order is reversed because the preceding account concerns people’s affairs and actions on earth.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Samarrai says al-samāʾ may mean one heaven or anything above, including clouds, rain, and the atmosphere; the broader sense is more inclusive than al-samāwāt and suits Yunus’s exhaustive scope.
rows.anchor: في موضع سابق أن (السماء) في القرآن تستعمل على معنيين

words: وَلاَ أَصْغَرُ مِن ذَلِكَ وَلاَ أَكْبَرُ
وَلاَ أَصْغَرَ مِن ذلك ولا أَكْبَرَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saba has the nominative with ordinary lā, while Yunus uses the accusative with lā of genus negation, whose exhaustive force suits the verse’s comprehensive account of divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: وجاء في آية سبأ بـ (لا) النافية التي لا تنص على الاستغراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinct wording in Nahl and Anam follows their different contexts: Nahl refutes shirk and false gods, while Anam addresses fabricated rules about food and livestock.
rows.anchor: إنّ سياق النحل في الرد على الشرك والنعي على المعبودات الباطلة من دون الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nahl says “worship,” includes “we,” adds “besides Him,” and says earlier people did likewise; Anam says “associate,” omits “we,” shortens the prohibition phrase, and calls earlier people liars, matching each sūra’s theme.
rows.anchor: حرمنا من دونه مِنْ شيء حرمنا من شيء
